usage: 여자친구가 또 토라졌어요.
My girlfriend got in a huff again.
Classic relationship word — partner gets quietly upset and goes cold.
사소한 일에 토라지지 마.
Don't sulk over little things.
친구/연인 사이 반말. The 'turn away and go silent' nuance is built in.
examples: 내가 농담한 걸 갖고 하루 종일 토라져 있었어.
She sulked all day over a joke I made.
토라져 있다 = staying in the sulking state for a while.
뭐 때문에 토라진 거야? 말을 해 줘야 알지.
What are you sulking about? You have to tell me so I know.
Very natural thing to say to a sulking partner.
선물 받고 금방 기분이 풀려서 더 이상 안 토라졌어요.
She got a gift and cheered up, so she stopped sulking.
기분이 풀리다 = mood un-knots; pairs naturally with 토라지다.
nuance: 토라지다 is the sulk where someone gets hurt or annoyed and pointedly turns cold — going quiet, looking away, giving you the silent treatment. It's softer and more passive than 화내다 (openly angry); the person isn't yelling, they're withdrawing. Extremely common in describing couples, close friends, or kids who feel slighted.
mistakes: Don't confuse with 화내다 — 토라지다 is sulking/pouting silently, not actively shouting. If someone is loudly angry, use 화내다.

english: to get in a huff (and sulk)
usage: 야, 삐쳤어?
Hey, are you upset (with me)?
The single most common way to ask if a friend is sulking. Casual.
그런 걸로 삐치지 마세요.
Don't get all huffy over something like that.
Gently telling someone they're overreacting and sulking.
examples: 내가 답장 늦게 했다고 삐쳤어.
He got in a huff because I replied late.
Texting culture — late replies genuinely cause people to 삐치다.
삐친 거 아니야? 목소리가 왜 그래?
Aren't you upset? Why do you sound like that?
Reading a sulky tone in someone's voice.
금방 삐치고 금방 풀리는 성격이에요.
He gets in a huff easily and gets over it just as fast.
Describing a personality that sulks quickly but doesn't hold grudges.
nuance: 삐치다 (often spelled/spoken 삐지다) is the everyday word for getting in a sulky huff because your feelings were hurt — someone forgot you, replied late, or left you out. It's lighter and more childish/cute than serious anger, used constantly among friends and couples. 토라지다 emphasizes turning away coldly; 삐치다 just emphasizes the hurt-and-pouty state.
mistakes: 삐지다 is the very common spoken variant; both are widely used, but 삐치다 is the standard dictionary form.
Past tense is 삐쳤어요 (삐치 + 었 → 삐쳐 + ㅆ). Don't write it as 삐쳣어요 or 삐쳤써요.

usage: 그만 좀 골내!
Quit being sulky/grumpy!
Reads as 'stop pouting in a grumpy mood'. Casual command.
애도 아니고 그런 걸로 골내요?
You're not a kid — are you really getting sulky over that?
Calling out childish grumpiness.
examples: 게임에서 졌다고 혼자 골내고 있어.
He's off by himself sulking because he lost the game.
골내다 = a moody, irritated sulk; pairs with 혼자 (alone).
동생이 골낸 표정으로 방에 들어가 버렸어요.
My younger sibling went into the room with a sulky, grumpy face.
골낸 표정 = a sullen/grumpy expression.
사소한 일로 골내지 말고 그냥 얘기해.
Don't get all grumpy over a small thing — just talk it out.
Encouraging communication instead of sulking.
nuance: 골내다 combines being sulky and being irritated — a grumpy, moody upset where someone broods and gives off a sour mood, half-pouting and half-angry. It's stronger and grumpier than 삐치다 but less explosive than 화내다. You'll also hear 골나다 (the intransitive 'to become grumpy') and the noun 골 in 골이 났다.
mistakes: 골내다 (transitive, 'to put out grumpiness') vs 골나다 (to become grumpy) — keep the 내/나 distinction like 화내다/화나다.
Don't confuse 골 (mood/temper here) with 골 meaning 'brain' or 'goal' — context decides.

usage: 나한테 짜증내지 마.
Don't take your irritation out on me.
Hugely common. The 'directed at me' meaning comes from 한테.
왜 자꾸 짜증내요?
Why do you keep snapping/getting irritated?
자꾸 (repeatedly) makes it feel like nagging irritation.
examples: 배고프면 나도 모르게 짜증내게 돼요.
When I'm hungry I end up getting irritable without realizing it.
Very relatable; -게 되다 = end up doing.
사장님이 직원들한테 짜증내서 분위기가 안 좋았어.
The boss snapped at the staff, so the mood was bad.
Workplace scene — extremely natural usage.
짜증내지 말고 차분하게 설명해 줄래?
Could you explain calmly instead of getting irritated?
Contrasts 짜증내다 with 차분하다 (calm).
nuance: 짜증내다 is to outwardly express irritation/annoyance — snapping, a sharp tone, an exasperated face. It's one of the most-used emotion verbs in daily life, lighter than full anger (화내다) but clearly negative and aimed at someone. Compare 짜증나다 ('to feel/get annoyed', the internal feeling) with 짜증내다 ('to act annoyed at someone').
mistakes: 짜증내다 (show irritation, transitive-ish) vs 짜증나다 (feel irritated). '나 짜증나' = I'm annoyed; '나한테 짜증내지 마' = don't be snippy at me.
Romanize the double ㅉ as 'jj' — it's a tense consonant, not 'j'.

usage: 애가 장난감 사 달라고 떼써요.
The kid is throwing a fit demanding I buy a toy.
The textbook scene for 떼쓰다 — a child's nagging demand.
떼쓴다고 다 되는 거 아니야.
Throwing a tantrum doesn't get you everything.
Said to a child (or jokingly to an adult acting like one).
examples: 마트에서 과자 사 달라고 바닥에 누워서 떼썼어요.
He lay on the floor at the mart demanding snacks.
떼썼어요 = past (떼쓰 + 었, ㅡ drops). Very vivid kid behavior.
어른이 돼서까지 떼쓰면 안 되지.
You can't keep throwing tantrums now that you're an adult.
Playfully scolding adult stubbornness.
아무리 떼써도 안 되는 건 안 돼.
No matter how much you whine for it, no means no.
Firm boundary-setting language with kids.
nuance: 떼쓰다 is to insistently, unreasonably demand something — the whining, foot-stamping, won't-take-no kind of behavior, prototypically by a child but also said of adults acting childishly. It centers on stubborn demanding rather than sadness or quiet sulking. Pairs constantly with -아/어 달라고 (asking for something to be done).
mistakes: 쓰다 here follows the ㅡ-irregular: stem 떼쓰- + 어 → 떼써, past 떼썼어요. Don't write 떼쓰어요.
It's 떼쓰다, not 때쓰다 — the vowel is ㅔ (떼 = a fit/unreasonable demand).

usage: 아기가 배고픈지 계속 보채요.
The baby keeps fussing — maybe it's hungry.
The core use: a baby crying/fussing for attention or a need.
그만 좀 보채, 곧 도착해.
Stop pestering me, we'll be there soon.
Said when someone keeps nagging 'are we there yet?'
examples: 애가 밤새 보채서 한숨도 못 잤어요.
The baby fussed all night so I didn't sleep a wink.
보채다 + 한숨도 못 자다 = a classic exhausted-parent line.
빨리 가자고 옆에서 자꾸 보채니까 정신이 없어.
He keeps pestering me to hurry, so I can't focus.
보채다 of an impatient adult nagging you to rush.
뭐가 그렇게 급하다고 보채요?
What's so urgent that you keep pestering me?
Pushing back on someone's impatient nagging.
nuance: 보채다 has two everyday senses: a baby/young child fretting and crying for a need, and a person impatiently pestering or nagging you to hurry or give them something. Both share the feel of restless, repeated fussing. Unlike 떼쓰다 (a stubborn specific demand), 보채다 leans more toward restless whining/urging.
mistakes: 보채 + 어 contracts to 보채 (보채요), past 보챘어요 — don't write 보채어요.
Mostly used for babies or impatient pestering; it's not a word for adult 'anger'.

usage: 우는 아이를 달래고 있어요.
I'm soothing the crying child.
The prototypical use — calming a crying kid.
삐친 친구 좀 달래 줘.
Go cheer up / smooth things over with the friend who's sulking.
달래다 toward a sulking person = win them back, calm them.
examples: 사탕으로 달래도 울음을 안 그쳤어요.
Even soothing him with candy didn't stop the crying.
달래도 = even though (I) soothe; pairs with 울음을 그치다.
화난 고객을 달래느라 진땀을 뺐어요.
I broke a sweat trying to calm down the angry customer.
Service-job reality; 달래다 also covers placating people.
속상한 마음을 달래려고 매운 음식을 먹었어요.
I ate spicy food to soothe my upset feelings.
마음을 달래다 = to comfort/soothe one's own heart.
nuance: 달래다 is to soothe, comfort, or placate someone who is crying, upset, or angry — and also to calm your own feelings (마음을 달래다). It's the natural counterpart to 울다, 토라지다, 떼쓰다: someone gets upset, and you 달래다 them. Warm and caring in tone.
mistakes: 달래 + 어 contracts to 달래 (달래요), past 달랬어요 — never 달래어요.
달래다 (to soothe) is unrelated to the homophone 달래 (a wild chive); context makes it clear.

usage: 등을 토닥여 줬어요.
I gave their back a comforting pat.
토닥이다 + 주다 = pat someone to comfort them. Etiquette: a warm gesture.
어깨 토닥여 주면서 위로했어요.
I comforted them, patting their shoulder.
Pairs naturally with 위로하다.
examples: 울지 말라고 아이 등을 토닥여 줬어요.
I patted the child's back, telling them not to cry.
토닥였어요 (past) = 토닥이 + 었; ㅣ+어 → 여.
수고했다며 어깨를 토닥여 주셨어요.
He patted my shoulder, saying I'd worked hard.
A very Korean gesture of recognition/comfort from a senior.
힘든 하루 끝에 스스로를 토닥여 주세요.
At the end of a hard day, give yourself a comforting pat.
스스로를 토닥이다 = self-comfort; common in self-care talk.
nuance: 토닥이다 is the soft, rhythmic comforting pat — on a back, shoulder, or head — that says 'it's okay, you did well.' It's a physical act of consolation, almost always with 주다 to show you're doing it for someone. Slightly stronger/repeated companion 다독이다 overlaps closely; 토닥이다 emphasizes the literal patting motion.
mistakes: 이다-ending verb: 토닥이 + 어 → 토닥여, past 토닥였어요. Don't write 토닥이어요.
Don't confuse the action 토닥이다 with the sound-symbolic adverb 토닥토닥 (the patting sound), though they're related.

usage: 힘들어하는 친구를 다독여 줬어요.
I comforted and reassured my struggling friend.
다독이다 = comfort + steady someone emotionally. Often with 주다.
스스로를 너무 다그치지 말고 다독여 주세요.
Don't push yourself too hard — be kind and reassure yourself.
Sets up the nice contrast 다그치다 vs 다독이다.
examples: 실패한 후배를 다독이며 다시 해 보라고 했어요.
I reassured the junior who'd failed and told them to try again.
다독이며 = while comforting; -으며 connective.
엄마가 등을 다독여 주니까 마음이 놓였어요.
When Mom patted my back reassuringly, I felt at ease.
다독였어요/다독여 주다 — 마음이 놓이다 = to feel relieved.
팀원들을 다독여서 분위기를 다시 살렸어요.
I rallied the team members and revived the mood.
다독이다 can mean to encourage/steady a group, not just one person.
nuance: 다독이다 means to comfort and steady someone — gently patting while reassuring them so they calm down and feel supported. It's warmer and more emotional than the purely physical 토닥이다, and it often implies pulling someone back together (다독여서 분위기를 살리다). Frequently paired with 위로하다 and 격려하다.
mistakes: 이다-ending: 다독이 + 어 → 다독여, past 다독였어요. Not 다독이어요.
다독이다 (comfort) is different from 다그치다 (to press/push someone) — they're near-opposites, so don't mix them up.

usage: 힘내라고 격려해 줬어요.
I encouraged them, saying 'hang in there.'
격려하다 + 주다 = encourage someone. Slightly formal/warm.
서로 격려하면서 준비했어요.
We prepared while encouraging each other.
서로 격려하다 = mutual encouragement; common in teams.
examples: 시험 떨어진 친구를 격려해 주고 싶었어요.
I wanted to encourage my friend who failed the exam.
Pairs with 떨어지다 (to fail); -아/어 주고 싶다 = want to do for.
감독님이 선수들을 격려하는 연설을 했어요.
The coach gave a speech encouraging the players.
격려하다 is the go-to verb for pep talks and speeches.
힘든 시기에 격려해 주셔서 정말 감사했어요.
Thank you so much for encouraging me during a hard time.
Polite gratitude; very natural in messages to mentors/seniors.
nuance: 격려하다 is to encourage or cheer someone on with words — a pep talk, a 'you can do it,' a supportive message during a hard time. It's a notch more formal and verbal than 응원하다 (to root for/cheer) and than the physical comforting of 다독이다. Common in work, sports, and study contexts.
mistakes: Pronounced/romanized 'gyeongnyeohada' — the ㄱㄹ in 격려 nasalizes to [경녀], so don't say 'gyeok-lyeo'.
격려하다 is encouragement in words; for physically comforting someone, reach for 다독이다 / 토닥이다 instead.

usage: 엄마한테 야단맞았어요.
I got told off by my mom.
Note the partner verb 야단맞다 = to get scolded (the receiving side).
애를 너무 야단치지 마세요.
Don't scold the kid too harshly.
Gentle advice to a parent.
examples: 선생님이 떠든 학생들을 야단쳤어요.
The teacher scolded the students who were being noisy.
야단쳤어요 (past) = 야단치 + 었; ㅣ+어 → 쳐.
거짓말한 걸 알고 부모님이 크게 야단치셨어요.
When they found out I lied, my parents scolded me a lot.
크게 야단치다 = to scold severely; -시- adds respect for parents.
야단치기보다 차분히 타이르는 게 나아요.
It's better to gently reason with them than to scold.
Contrasts 야단치다 with 타이르다 (to admonish gently).
nuance: 야단치다 is to scold or tell someone off — a parent, teacher, or boss reprimanding a child or junior for doing wrong. It's stronger and more authority-driven than just 화내다 (being angry), and it implies a power gap (older/senior to younger). The flip side, being on the receiving end, is 야단맞다 / 혼나다.
mistakes: 치다-ending: 야단치 + 어 → 야단쳐, past 야단쳤어요. Don't write 야단치어요.
Use 야단치다 from the scolder's side; for 'I got scolded' use 야단맞다 or 혼나다, not 야단치다.

usage: 내 꿈을 비웃지 마.
Don't sneer at my dream.
비웃다 takes a direct object (꿈을, 사람을). Hurtful nuance.
사람들이 내 실수를 비웃었어요.
People laughed at my mistake (mockingly).
Scornful laughter, not friendly laughter.
examples: 발음이 이상하다고 비웃을까 봐 말을 못 했어요.
I couldn't speak up, afraid they'd laugh at my pronunciation.
Very real fear for language learners; -을까 봐 = afraid that.
남을 비웃는 사람은 결국 신뢰를 잃어요.
People who sneer at others end up losing trust.
Moral-tone sentence; 남을 비웃다 = mock others.
콧방귀를 뀌며 내 계획을 비웃었어요.
He scoffed and sneered at my plan.
콧방귀를 뀌다 (to scoff) pairs idiomatically with 비웃다.
nuance: 비웃다 is to laugh at someone scornfully — to mock, sneer, or ridicule, looking down on them. The 비- prefix (from 비방/비하 nuance) turns plain 웃다 (to laugh) into contemptuous laughter. It's distinctly negative and hurtful, unlike 놀리다 which can be playful teasing.
mistakes: 웃다 keeps its ㅅ (it is NOT a ㅅ-irregular): 비웃어요, 비웃었어요 — never 비웄어요.
비웃다 is scornful/mean; for light, friendly teasing use 놀리다 instead, or you'll sound harsher than intended.
